claim: Ookinete traversal of the Anopheles gambiae midgut disrupts the barriers that normally prevent bacteria of the gut microbiota from coming in direct contact with epithelial cells.
source: Ookinete traversal of the Anopheles gambiae midgut disrupts the barriers that normally prevent bacteria of the gut microbiota from coming in direct contact with epithelial cells (Kumar et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by citation to Kumar et al., 2010

claim: Ookinete traversal of the Anopheles gambiae midgut attracts hemocytes to the basal surface of the midgut.
source: Ookinete traversal of the Anopheles gambiae midgut disrupts the barriers that normally prevent bacteria of the gut microbiota from coming in direct contact with epithelial cells (Kumar et al., 2010), and this attracts hemocytes to the basal surface of the midgut (Barletta et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Barletta et al., 2019

claim: Plasmodium ookinetes cause irreversible damage to the cells they invade.
source: Plasmodium ookinetes also cause irreversible damage to the cells they invade and trigger a strong caspase-mediated nitration response (Han et al., 2000; Oliveira et al., 2012, Trisnadi and Barillas-Mury, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Han et al., 2000; Oliveira et al., 2012, Trisnadi and Barillas-Mury, 2020

claim: Plasmodium ookinetes trigger a strong caspase-mediated nitration response.
source: Plasmodium ookinetes also cause irreversible damage to the cells they invade and trigger a strong caspase-mediated nitration response (Han et al., 2000; Oliveira et al., 2012, Trisnadi and Barillas-Mury, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Han et al., 2000; Oliveira et al., 2012, Trisnadi and Barillas-Mury, 2020

claim: When hemocytes come in contact with a nitrated midgut surface, they undergo apoptosis and release hemocyte-derived microvesicles (HdMv).
source: When hemocytes come in contact with a nitrated midgut surface, they undergo apoptosis and release hemocyte-derived microvesicles (HdMv) (Castillo et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Castillo et al., 2017

claim: Local HdMv release promotes activation of thioester containing-protein 1 (TEP1).
source: Local HdMv release promotes activation of thioester containing-protein 1 (TEP1) (Castillo et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citation to Castillo et al., 2017

claim: TEP1 is a major final effector of the mosquito complement-like system that binds to the parasite's surface and forms a complex that lyses the ookinete.
source: Local HdMv release promotes activation of thioester containing-protein 1 (TEP1) (Castillo et al., 2017), a major final effector of the mosquito complement-like system that binds to the parasite's surface and forms a complex that lyses the ookinete (Blandin et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Blandin et al., 2004

claim: Mosquito hemocytes are classified into three cell types based on their morphology: prohemocytes, oenocytoids, and granulocytes.
source: Mosquito hemocytes are classified into three cell types, prohemocytes, oenocytoids, and granulocytes, based on their morphology.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about mosquito hemocyte classification

claim: Single-cell RNA sequencing (sc-RNAseq) analysis of A. gambiae hemocytes identified several novel subpopulations of granulocytes based on their transcriptional profiles.
source: However, single-cell RNA sequencing (sc-RNAseq) analysis of A. gambiae hemocytes identified several novel subpopulations of granulocytes based on their transcriptional profiles and defined molecular markers specific for hemocyte subpopulations (Raddi et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Raddi et al., 2020

claim: Single-cell RNA sequencing analysis defined molecular markers specific for hemocyte subpopulations.
source: However, single-cell RNA sequencing (sc-RNAseq) analysis of A. gambiae hemocytes identified several novel subpopulations of granulocytes based on their transcriptional profiles and defined molecular markers specific for hemocyte subpopulations (Raddi et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Raddi et al., 2020

claim: Regular granulocytes derive from prohemocytes.
source: Furthermore, Lineage analysis revealed that regular granulocytes derive from prohemocytes and can further differentiate into distinct cell types, including dividing granulocytes, and two final effector cells, megacytes and antimicrobial (AM) granulocytes (Raddi et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Raddi et al., 2020

claim: Regular granulocytes can further differentiate into distinct cell types, including dividing granulocytes, megacytes, and antimicrobial (AM) granulocytes.
source: Furthermore, Lineage analysis revealed that regular granulocytes derive from prohemocytes and can further differentiate into distinct cell types, including dividing granulocytes, and two final effector cells, megacytes and antimicrobial (AM) granulocytes (Raddi et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Raddi et al., 2020

claim: Silencing Cactus in A. gambiae mosquitoes elicits a very strong TEP1-mediated immune response that eliminates Plasmodium berghei ookinetes.
source: Silencing Cactus, a negative regulator of Toll signaling in A. gambiae mosquitoes, elicits a very strong TEP1-mediated immune response that eliminates Plasmodium berghei ookinetes (Frolet et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Frolet et al., 2006

claim: Co-silencing Cactus with either TEP1 or the Rel1 transcription factor rescues the phenotype of Cactus silencing.
source: This phenotype can be rescued by co-silencing Cactus with either TEP1 or the Rel1 transcription factor, indicating that parasite elimination is mediated by activation of Toll signaling, with TEP1 as a final effector (Frolet et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Frolet et al., 2006

claim: Parasite elimination in Cactus-silenced mosquitoes is mediated by activation of Toll signaling, with TEP1 as a final effector.
source: This phenotype can be rescued by co-silencing Cactus with either TEP1 or the Rel1 transcription factor, indicating that parasite elimination is mediated by activation of Toll signaling, with TEP1 as a final effector (Frolet et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Frolet et al., 2006 and logical inference from rescue experiments

claim: Hemocytes mediate the enhanced immune response in Cactus-silenced mosquitoes.
source: Later studies showed that hemocytes mediate this enhanced immune response, as transfer of Cactus-silenced hemocytes into naïve mosquitoes recapitulates the phenotype of systemic Cactus silencing (Ramirez et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ramirez et al., 2014

claim: Transfer of Cactus-silenced hemocytes into naïve mosquitoes recapitulates the phenotype of systemic Cactus silencing.
source: Later studies showed that hemocytes mediate this enhanced immune response, as transfer of Cactus-silenced hemocytes into naïve mosquitoes recapitulates the phenotype of systemic Cactus silencing (Ramirez et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ramirez et al., 2014

claim: Cactus silencing increases HdMv release in response to ookinete midgut invasion.
source: Furthermore, Cactus silencing also increases HdMv release in response to ookinete midgut invasion (Castillo et al., 2017), indicating that hemocytes are more reactive to Plasmodium infection.
evidence: Supported by citation to Castillo et al., 2017

claim: Hemocytes in Cactus-silenced mosquitoes are more reactive to Plasmodium infection.
source: Furthermore, Cactus silencing also increases HdMv release in response to ookinete midgut invasion (Castillo et al., 2017), indicating that hemocytes are more reactive to Plasmodium infection.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Cactus silencing increases HdMv release

claim: Bulk sequencing of cDNA libraries from hemocytes generated between 16.2 and 25.3 million fragments that mapped to the A. gambiae AgamP4.9 transcriptome.
source: Bulk sequencing of cDNA libraries generated between 16.2 and 25.3 million fragments that mapped to the A. gambiae AgamP4.9 transcriptome.
evidence: Direct experimental data from sequencing

claim: A total of 9421 unique transcripts were included in the analysis after filtering for transcripts with 10 or more reads.
source: Only transcripts with 10 or more reads were included in the analysis, resulting in a total of 9421 unique transcripts (https://www.ebi.ac.uk/biostudies/arrayexpress/studies/E-MTAB-11252).
evidence: Direct experimental data from sequencing analysis

claim: The differences in expression between dsLacZ versus dsCactus-silenced hemocytes explained 81% of the variance between the four experimental groups.
source: Glass-bound and unbound hemocyte samples were analyzed together, because the differences in expression between dsLacZ versus dsCactus-silenced hemocytes explained 81% of the variance between the four experimental groups (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B

claim: Differential expression analysis of Cactus-silenced hemocytes identified 1071 differentially expressed genes (Q value <0.001).
source: Differential expression (DE) analysis of Cactus-silenced hemocytes using the DESeq2 software identified 1071 differentially expressed genes (Q value <0.001), of which 407 were upregulated (log2 fold change >2), while 664 were downregulated (log2 fold change <−2) (Figure 1A).
evidence: Direct experimental data from differential expression analysis shown in Figure 1A

claim: 407 genes were upregulated (log2 fold change >2) in Cactus-silenced hemocytes.
source: Differential expression (DE) analysis of Cactus-silenced hemocytes using the DESeq2 software identified 1071 differentially expressed genes (Q value <0.001), of which 407 were upregulated (log2 fold change >2), while 664 were downregulated (log2 fold change <−2) (Figure 1A).
evidence: Direct experimental data from differential expression analysis shown in Figure 1A

claim: 664 genes were downregulated (log2 fold change <−2) in Cactus-silenced hemocytes.
source: Differential expression (DE) analysis of Cactus-silenced hemocytes using the DESeq2 software identified 1071 differentially expressed genes (Q value <0.001), of which 407 were upregulated (log2 fold change >2), while 664 were downregulated (log2 fold change <−2) (Figure 1A).
evidence: Direct experimental data from differential expression analysis shown in Figure 1A

claim: 23 oenocytoid markers, 2 prohemocyte markers, and 57 granulocyte markers were differentially expressed between dsLacZ and dsCactus hemocytes.
source: Overall, 23 oenocytoid markers, 2 from prohemocytes, and 57 from granulocytes were differentially expressed between dsLacZ and dsCactus hemocytes (Supplementary file 1 and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Direct experimental data from differential expression analysis

claim: Most differentially expressed oenocytoid markers (22/23, 95%) were downregulated in Cactus-silenced hemocytes.
source: Most differentially expressed oenocytoid markers 22/23 (95%) were downregulated, while one of the prohemocyte markers was upregulated and the other one was downregulated (Figure 1B).
evidence: Direct experimental data shown in Figure 1B

claim: The number of downregulated granulocyte markers (28/57, 49%) was very similar to that of upregulated ones (29/57, 51%).
source: The number of downregulated granulocyte markers 28/57 (49%) was very similar to that of upregulated ones 29/57 (51%).
evidence: Direct experimental data from differential expression analysis

claim: Most upregulated granulocyte markers (18/29, 62%) correspond to megacytes.
source: However, detailed analysis of granulocyte subpopulations revealed that most upregulated markers 18/29 (62%) correspond to megacytes, while most downregulated markers correspond to regular granulocytes 21/28 (75%).
evidence: Direct experimental data from differential expression analysis

claim: Most downregulated granulocyte markers (21/28, 75%) correspond to regular granulocytes.
source: However, detailed analysis of granulocyte subpopulations revealed that most upregulated markers 18/29 (62%) correspond to megacytes, while most downregulated markers correspond to regular granulocytes 21/28 (75%).
evidence: Direct experimental data from differential expression analysis

claim: dsCactus silencing increases the proportion of circulating megacytes, at the expense of a reduction in regular granulocytes.
source: This suggests that dsCactus silencing increases the proportion of circulating megacytes, at the expense of a reduction in regular granulocytes.
evidence: Inferred from the differential expression data showing upregulation of megacyte markers and downregulation of regular granulocyte markers

claim: Expression of several genes involved in Toll signaling or final effectors of this pathway are upregulated in dsCactus hemocytes.
source: As expected, expression of several genes involved in Toll signaling or final effector this pathway, such as Toll-like receptors, CLIP proteases, Serpins, C-type Lectins, and Defensin are upregulated in dsCactus hemocytes (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Direct experimental data from differential expression analysis

claim: Cactus silencing did not significantly increase the proportion of total circulating granulocytes based on hemocyte counts by light microscopy.
source: Cactus silencing did not significantly increase the proportion of total circulating granulocytes, based on hemocyte counts by light microscopy (Figure 2—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Direct experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: Cactus silencing dramatically increased the proportion of large granulocytes (diameter >40 µm) from 5.3% to 79.2% (p < 0.0001).
source: Cactus silencing dramatically increased the proportion of large granulocytes (diameter >40 µm), presumably megacytes, from 5.3% to 79.2% (p < 0.0001, X2 test) (Figure 2A, B)
evidence: Direct experimental data shown in Figure 2A, B with statistical analysis

claim: Megacytes from Cactus-silenced mosquitoes have an average diameter of 47 µm after spreading on a glass surface.
source: Interestingly, megacytes from Cactus-silenced mosquitoes (Figure 2A) are even larger (average diameter of 47 µm after spreading in a glass surface) than megacytes from dsLacZ controls (average diameter of 30 µm) (Figure 2C, D).
evidence: Direct experimental data shown in Figure 2C, D

claim: Megacytes from dsLacZ controls have an average diameter of 30 µm after spreading on a glass surface.
source: Interestingly, megacytes from Cactus-silenced mosquitoes (Figure 2A) are even larger (average diameter of 47 µm after spreading in a glass surface) than megacytes from dsLacZ controls (average diameter of 30 µm) (Figure 2C, D).
evidence: Direct experimental data shown in Figure 2C, D

claim: The proportion of TM7318-positive granulocytes was much higher (80%) in Cactus-silenced females than in dsLacZ controls (4%) (p < 0.0001).
source: In situ RNA hybridization of dsCactus granulocytes with a fluorescent probe for the megacyte-specific marker TM7318, confirmed that the proportion of TM7318-positive granulocytes was much higher (80%) in Cactus-silenced females than in dsLacZ controls (4%) (p < 0.0001, X2 test) (Figure 2E, F)
evidence: Direct experimental data from in situ RNA hybridization shown in Figure 2E, F

claim: Overactivation of Toll signaling triggers a dramatic increase in the proportion of circulating megacytes.
source: In situ RNA hybridization of dsCactus granulocytes with a fluorescent probe for the megacyte-specific marker TM7318, confirmed that the proportion of TM7318-positive granulocytes was much higher (80%) in Cactus-silenced females than in dsLacZ controls (4%) (p < 0.0001, X2 test) (Figure 2E, F), providing direct evidence that overactivation of Toll signaling triggers a dramatic increase in the proportion of circulating megacytes.
evidence: Direct evidence from in situ RNA hybridization data shown in Figure 2E, F

claim: TM7318 mRNA levels were 42-fold higher in dsCactus hemocytes than the dsLacZ control group (p < 0.001).
source: Expression analysis of the TM7318 marker in perfused hemocyte samples confirmed that mRNA levels were 42-fold higher in dsCactus hemocytes than the dsLacZ control group (p < 0.001, T-test) (Figure 2G)
evidence: Direct experimental data from expression analysis shown in Figure 2G

claim: FBN50 mRNA levels showed a modest increase (2.8-fold) in dsCactus hemocytes (p < 0.0001).
source: Expression analysis of the TM7318 marker in perfused hemocyte samples confirmed that mRNA levels were 42-fold higher in dsCactus hemocytes than the dsLacZ control group (p < 0.001, T-test) (Figure 2G), while a modest increase (2.8-fold) in FBN50 mRNA, a marker of AM effector granulocytes, was observed (p < 0.0001, T-test).
evidence: Direct experimental data from expression analysis shown in Figure 2G

claim: Expression of FBN11228, a marker of regular granulocytes, decreased by 30-fold in circulating hemocytes of Cactus-silenced mosquitoes.
source: Conversely, expression of FBN11228, a marker of regular granulocytes, decreased by 30-fold in circulating hemocytes of Cactus-silenced mosquitoes (Figure 2G).
evidence: Direct experimental data from expression analysis shown in Figure 2G

claim: The number of circulating hemocytes was not significantly different between dsLacZ (mean 17,151/mosquito) and dsCactus mosquitoes (mean 23,477/mosquito) 2 days post-injection.
source: A total hemocyte count revealed that the number of circulating hemocytes was not significantly different between dsLacZ (mean 17,151/mosquito, n = 14) and dsCactus mosquitoes (mean 23,477/mosquito, n = 14, Mann–Whitney T-test) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) 2 days post-injection.
evidence: Direct experimental data from hemocyte counts shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A

claim: The mean number of total hemocytes 4 days post-silencing was not significantly different between dsLacZ (mean 8725/mosquito) and dsCactus mosquitoes (mean 10,836/mosquito).
source: The mean number of total hemocytes was lower 4 days post-silencing, but there was also no significant difference between dsLacZ (mean 8725/mosquito, n = 14) and dsCactus mosquitoes (mean 10,836/mosquito, n = 14, Mann–Whitney T-test) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Direct experimental data from hemocyte counts shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A

claim: There was no difference in the proportion of granulocytes at 2 days between dsLacZ (3.62%) and dsCactus females (3.48%).
source: Furthermore, there was no difference in the proportion granulocytes at 2 days, dsLacZ (3.62%) and dsCactus females (3.48%, Mann–Whitney T-test), and 4 days, dsLacZ (3.91%) and dsCactus females (5.47%, Mann–Whitney T-test), post-injection.
evidence: Direct experimental data from hemocyte counts

claim: A significant increase in the proportion of megacytes was already apparent 2 days post-injection in Cactus-silenced mosquitoes (2.08% of all hemocytes, p < 0.0001), relative to dsLacZ controls (0.07%).
source: In contrast, a significant increase in the proportion of megacyte was already apparent 2 days post-injection in Cactus-silenced mosquitoes (2.08% of all hemocytes, p < 0.0001, Mann–Whitney T-test), relative to dsLacZ controls (0.07%) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: Direct experimental data from hemocyte counts shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B

claim: At 4 days post-injection, the proportion of megacytes reached 3.7% in Cactus-silenced mosquitoes (p < 0.0001) relative to dsLacZ controls (0.07%).
source: At 4 days post-injection, the differences were more pronounced, with the proportion of megacytes reaching 3.7% in Cactus-silenced mosquitoes (p < 0.0001, Mann–Whitney T-test) relative to dsLacZ controls (0.07%) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: Direct experimental data from hemocyte counts shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C

claim: The total number of hemocytes and the percentage of total granulocytes remained unchanged in response to dsCactus silencing, but the proportion of megacytes increased at the expense of other granulocytes.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that, although the total number of hemocytes and the percentage of total granulocytes remained unchanged in response to dsCactus silencing, the proportion of megacytes increased at the expense of other granulocytes.
evidence: Inferred from multiple hemocyte count measurements

claim: The proportion of BrdU+ hemocytes in dsCactus mosquitoes (51%, n = 694 cells) is not significantly different from dsLacZ controls (52%, n = 410 cells).
source: The proportion of BrdU+ hemocytes that adhered to glass (mostly granulocytes) in dsCactus mosquitoes (51%, n = 694 cells) is not significantly different from dsLacZ controls (52%, n = 410 cells) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A, B).
evidence: Direct experimental data from BrdU labeling shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A, B

claim: BrdU fluorescence intensity is not significantly different between dsLacZ and dsCactus hemocytes.
source: BrdU fluorescence intensity (RFU) is also not significantly different between dsLacZ and dsCactus hemocytes (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Direct experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C

claim: The ratio of BrdU fluorescence intensity to nuclear volume is significantly lower in dsCactus hemocytes.
source: However, the ratio of BrdU fluorescence intensity to nuclear volume is significantly lower in dsCactus hemocytes (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Direct experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2D

claim: The increase in nuclear volume in megacytes does not involve DNA replication.
source: This indicates that the increase in nuclear volume in megacytes does not involve DNA replication.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that BrdU fluorescence intensity to nuclear volume ratio is lower in dsCactus hemocytes

claim: Two days post-injection, the proportion of PHH3+ hemocytes in dsCactus mosquitoes (0.7%, n = 896) was not significantly different from dsLacZ controls (0.6%, n = 718 cells).
source: Two days post-injection, the proportion of PHH3+ hemocytes that adhered to glass (mostly granulocytes) in dsCactus mosquitoes (0.7%, n = 896) was small, and not significantly different from dsLacZ controls (0.6%, n = 718 cells) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Direct experimental data from PHH3 staining shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D

claim: At 4 days post-injection, the proportion of PHH3+ hemocytes was similar in dsLacZ (0.5%, n = 799 cells) and dsCactus (0.3%, n = 1039).
source: At 4 days the proportions were also similar, with very few hemocytes positive for PHH3 staining both in dsLacZ (0.5%, n = 799 cells) and dsCactus (0.3%, n = 1039) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Direct experimental data from PHH3 staining shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D

claim: The few hemocytes that were positive for PHH3 in dsCactus mosquitoes did not have the characteristic size or morphology of megacytes.
source: Moreover, the few hemocytes that were positive for PHH3 in dsCactus mosquitoes did not have the characteristic size or morphology of megacytes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Direct experimental observation from PHH3 staining shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D

claim: Cactus silencing promotes differentiation of granulocytes to the megacyte lineage.
source: These observations, together with the increase in the proportion of megacytes in dsCactus females, at the expense of other regular granulocytes (Figures 1B and 2G), indicate that Cactus silencing promotes differentiation of granulocytes to the megacyte lineage.
evidence: Inferred from multiple lines of evidence including cell counts, marker expression, and proliferation assays

claim: Regular granulocytes reach an average diameter of 14.2 μm when they spread over a glass surface.
source: Regular granulocytes (Figure 3A) reach an average diameter of 14.2 μm (Figure 3B) when they spread over a glass surface, while the average diameter of megacytes is 28.6 μm (p < 0.0001, unpaired T-test) (Figure 3A, B).
evidence: Direct experimental data shown in Figure 3A, B

claim: The average diameter of megacytes is 28.6 μm when they spread over a glass surface (p < 0.0001).
source: Regular granulocytes (Figure 3A) reach an average diameter of 14.2 μm (Figure 3B) when they spread over a glass surface, while the average diameter of megacytes is 28.6 μm (p < 0.0001, unpaired T-test) (Figure 3A, B).
evidence: Direct experimental data shown in Figure 3A, B

claim: Both regular granulocytes and megacytes attached to the glass surface and spread fully within 1 hr.
source: After perfusion, a green, fluorescent probe (Cell Mask) was added to label the plasma membrane. Both regular granulocytes and megacytes attached to the glass surface and spread fully within 1 hr (Videos 1–4).
evidence: Direct experimental observation from live imaging shown in Videos 1–4

claim: Megacytes already have a larger cell diameter when they first attach to glass.
source: Megacytes already have a larger cell diameter when they first attach to glass (Figure 3C, upper panel and Video 3)
evidence: Direct experimental observation from live imaging shown in Figure 3C and Video 3

claim: Megacytes exhibit a peripheral 'halo', corresponding to an area of extended thin cytoplasm, almost devoid of vesicles.
source: Megacytes already have a larger cell diameter when they first attach to glass (Figure 3C, upper panel and Video 3), and exhibit a peripheral 'halo', corresponding to an area of extended thin cytoplasm, almost devoid of vesicles (Figure 3C, upper panel and Video 3).
evidence: Direct experimental observation from live imaging shown in Figure 3C and Video 3

claim: Megacytes have a large nucleus and a voluminous cytoplasm in the central region of the cell that flattens dramatically as the cell 'spreads' over the glass surface.
source: Lateral views revealed that, initially, megacytes have a large nucleus and a voluminous cytoplasm in the central region of the cell that flattens dramatically as the cell 'spreads' over the glass surface (Figure 3C, lower panel and Video 4).
evidence: Direct experimental observation from live imaging shown in Figure 3C and Video 4

claim: The central region of regular granulocytes remains mostly unchanged during spreading.
source: In contrast, the central region of regular granulocytes remains mostly unchanged (Figure 3D, lower panel and Video 2)
evidence: Direct experimental observation from live imaging shown in Figure 3D and Video 2

claim: The periphery of regular granulocytes exhibits a modest increase in diameter as the cell spreads along the surface.
source: In contrast, the central region of regular granulocytes remains mostly unchanged (Figure 3D, lower panel and Video 2) and the periphery of the cell exhibits a modest increase in diameter as the cell spreads along the surface (Figure 3D, upper panel and Video 1).
evidence: Direct experimental observation from live imaging shown in Figure 3D and Video 1

claim: Circulating hemocytes in dsLacZ females have a smaller diameter than those of dsCactus females.
source: Circulating hemocytes in dsLacZ females (presumably normal granulocytes) have a smaller diameter than those of dsCactus females (Videos 5 and 6; Figure 3A, B)
evidence: Direct experimental observation from in vivo live imaging shown in Videos 5 and 6, and Figure 3A, B

claim: Hemocytes from dsLacZ females seldom come in contact with each other as they patrol the basal surface of the midgut.
source: Circulating hemocytes in dsLacZ females (presumably normal granulocytes) have a smaller diameter than those of dsCactus females (Videos 5 and 6; Figure 3A, B), and they seldom come in contact with each other as they patrol the basal surface of the midgut (Video 5).
evidence: Direct experimental observation from in vivo live imaging shown in Video 5

claim: Hemocytes from dsCactus females are larger and have a spindle shape.
source: Hemocytes from dsCactus females (presumably megacytes) are larger and have a spindle shape (Figure 3A, B; Videos 3 and 4).
evidence: Direct experimental observation from live imaging shown in Figure 3A, B and Videos 3 and 4

claim: Hemocytes from dsCactus females have higher plasticity and can readily stretch their cytoplasm.
source: They appear to have higher plasticity, as they can readily stretch their cytoplasm and often come into contact with each other (Video 6).
evidence: Direct experimental observation from in vivo live imaging shown in Video 6

claim: Hemocytes from dsCactus females often come into contact with each other.
source: They appear to have higher plasticity, as they can readily stretch their cytoplasm and often come into contact with each other (Video 6).
evidence: Direct experimental observation from in vivo live imaging shown in Video 6

claim: Some megacytes from dsCactus mosquitoes projected long thin filopodia toward other megacytes.
source: The plasticity of dsCactus megacytes was confirmed by in vitro live imaging of perfused hemocytes labeled by systemic injection of Vybrant CM-DiI and green Cell Mask. Some megacytes from dsCactus mosquitoes projected long thin filopodia toward other megacytes (Video 7).
evidence: Direct experimental observation from in vitro live imaging shown in Video 7

claim: The process of projecting long thin filopodia was not observed in regular granulocytes or in megacytes from the dsLacZ controls.
source: This process was not observed in regular granulocytes or in megacytes from the dsLacZ controls.
evidence: Direct experimental observation from live imaging

claim: dsCactus megacytes are more active, have increased plasticity as they patrol the midgut, and greater tendency to interact with each other and form clusters.
source: Taken together, our live imaging data indicate that, in addition to their larger diameter (Figure 2C, D), dsCactus megacytes are also more active, have increased plasticity as they patrol the midgut (Video 6), and greater tendency to interact with each other and form clusters (Videos 6 and 7).
evidence: Inferred from multiple live imaging observations shown in Videos 6 and 7 and Figure 2C, D

claim: Regular granulocytes are significantly smaller (6–10 µm) than megacytes (15–20 µm) when fixed in suspension.
source: As expected, the maximum diameter of hemocytes fixed while in suspension was smaller than when they were allowed to spread on a glass surface. However, regular granulocytes were still significantly smaller (6–10 µm) than megacytes (15–20 µm), with nuclei that are also proportionally smaller (Figure 4A, B).
evidence: Direct experimental observation from TEM shown in Figure 4A, B

claim: Extensive electrodense areas are observed in the nuclei of megacytes, probably corresponding to the nucleolus.
source: Extensive electrodense areas are observed in the nuclei of megacytes, probably corresponding to the nucleolus.
evidence: Direct experimental observation from TEM with speculative interpretation

claim: Large numbers of cytoplasmic vacuoles that contain abundant amorphous material are observed in megacytes.
source: Large numbers of cytoplasmic vacuoles that contain abundant amorphous material are observed, as well as an extensive mitochondrial network (Figure 4A, B).
evidence: Direct experimental observation from TEM shown in Figure 4A, B

claim: Megacytes exhibit an extensive mitochondrial network.
source: Large numbers of cytoplasmic vacuoles that contain abundant amorphous material are observed, as well as an extensive mitochondrial network (Figure 4A, B).
evidence: Direct experimental observation from TEM shown in Figure 4A, B

claim: Large membrane-bound mitochondria-like extracellular structures and small vesicles are often observed 'budding off' from the surface of dsCactus megacytes.
source: It is noteworthy that large membrane-bound mitochondria-like extracellular structures and small vesicles are often observed 'budding off' from the surface of dsCactus megacytes (Figure 4B, C), but not from regular granulocytes (Figure 4A).
evidence: Direct experimental observation from TEM shown in Figure 4B, C

claim: Large membrane-bound mitochondria-like extracellular structures and small vesicles are not observed budding off from regular granulocytes.
source: It is noteworthy that large membrane-bound mitochondria-like extracellular structures and small vesicles are often observed 'budding off' from the surface of dsCactus megacytes (Figure 4B, C), but not from regular granulocytes (Figure 4A).
evidence: Direct experimental observation from TEM shown in Figure 4A

claim: Mitochondria of regular granulocytes have a punctate pattern with strong staining on individual organelles.
source: Mitochondria of regular granulocytes have a punctate pattern with strong staining on individual organelles (Figure 4D).
evidence: Direct experimental observation from Mitotracker staining shown in Figure 4D

claim: Megacytes exhibit a more diffuse and extensive mitochondrial network.
source: In contrast, megacytes exhibit a more diffuse and extensive mitochondrial network (Figure 4E).
evidence: Direct experimental observation from Mitotracker staining shown in Figure 4E

claim: Direct contact of bacteria with epithelial cells, before the peritrophic matrix is formed, triggers PGE2 release and attracts hemocytes to the basal surface of the midgut.
source: We have shown that direct contact of bacteria with epithelial cells, before the peritrophic matrix is formed, triggers PGE2 release and attracts hemocytes to the basal surface of the midgut (Barletta et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Barletta et al., 2019

claim: Bacterial feeding attracted hemocytes to the midgut surface in both dsCactus and dsLacZ control females.
source: As expected, bacterial feeding attracted hemocytes to the midgut surface in both dsCactus and dsLacZ control females (Figure 5A, B).
evidence: Direct experimental observation shown in Figure 5A, B
